learningObjectives.title: C4.2 Transfers of energy and matter

questions.q: A population is best defined as:
options: All the individuals of one species in an area at one time
All the organisms in an ecosystem
The living and non-living parts of a habitat
questions.explain: A community is all populations together; an ecosystem also includes the abiotic environment.

questions.q: In a sigmoid (S-shaped) population growth curve, growth slows and levels off as the population approaches:
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum population an environment can sustain, set by limiting factors.

questions.q: During the exponential phase of population growth:
options: Resources are abundant and growth is rapid
questions.explain: With plentiful resources and few limiting factors, the population grows rapidly.

questions.q: A close relationship in which one species benefits and the other is harmed is:
questions.explain: In parasitism the parasite benefits at the host's expense; in mutualism both benefit.

questions.q: An interaction in which both species benefit is:
questions.explain: For example, mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots exchange nutrients to mutual benefit.

questions.q: Ecologists estimate the size of a mobile animal population using the:
questions.explain: Mark–recapture uses the proportion of marked individuals recaptured to estimate total population size.

questions.q: Predator and prey populations often show linked cycles because:
options: A rise in prey supports more predators, which then reduce prey numbers
Predators have no effect on prey
questions.explain: This density-dependent feedback produces the characteristic out-of-phase oscillations.

questions.q: Organisms that make their own organic compounds using an external energy source are:
questions.explain: Producers (e.g. plants) form the base of food chains by fixing energy into organic molecules.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of energy is typically transferred from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explain: Roughly 90% of energy is lost between trophic levels (as heat, in respiration and undigested matter), so only ~10% passes on.

questions.q: Because energy is lost between trophic levels, food chains usually have:
options: A limited number of trophic levels
questions.explain: Energy loss limits the biomass and number of organisms that higher levels can support, capping chain length.

questions.q: Organisms that break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients are:
questions.explain: Decomposers (e.g. bacteria and fungi) release nutrients back into the ecosystem for reuse.

questions.q: In a pyramid of energy, each bar represents the energy:
options: Available at each trophic level per unit area per unit time
questions.explain: Pyramids of energy are always upright because energy decreases at each successive level.

questions.q: Carbon is returned from living organisms to the atmosphere mainly by:
questions.explain: Respiration releases CO2; photosynthesis removes it. Combustion and decomposition also return carbon to the atmosphere.

questions.q: Burning fossil fuels affects the carbon cycle by:
options: Adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere faster than it is removed
questions.explain: Combustion transfers long-stored carbon to the atmosphere, raising atmospheric CO2 and driving climate change.

questions.q: Two species competing for exactly the same limiting resource illustrate:
questions.explain: Competition between different species for a shared limited resource can reduce the growth of one or both.

questions.q: Competition between members of the same species is described as:
questions.explain: Intraspecific competition is often intense because individuals need identical resources.

questions.q: A food web is a more realistic model than a food chain because it:
options: Shows the many interconnected feeding relationships in a community
Shows energy increasing at each level
questions.explain: Most organisms have multiple food sources and consumers, which a web represents better than a single chain.

questions.q: A pyramid of numbers can appear inverted (small base) when:
options: A single large producer supports many primary consumers
questions.explain: For example, one oak tree supports many insects, so numbers (unlike energy) can give an inverted pyramid.

questions.q: Density-dependent factors that limit population growth include:
questions.explain: Density-dependent factors intensify as population density rises; density-independent factors (e.g. weather events) act regardless of density.

questions.q: Decomposers are essential to ecosystems because they:
options: Recycle nutrients from dead matter back to producers
questions.explain: Nutrient recycling by decomposers sustains producer growth, keeping matter cycling within the ecosystem.
